title: Exfiltration
summary: Exfiltration is the tactic covering the removal of data from the victim environment after it has been collected and staged, and it is usually the last point at which defenders can still prevent business harm rather than only measure it. Behaviours include transferring files over the existing command and control channel, uploading data to legitimate cloud storage, file-sharing, code-hosting, or webmail services, sending it over alternative protocols such as file transfer or mail, using physical media on endpoints, and throttling transfers to stay under volumetric alerting thresholds. Telemetry is abundant but concentrated at the boundary: proxy and web gateway logs with upload volume and destination category, netflow records showing large asymmetric transfers, data loss prevention alerts on content or volume, cloud audit logs recording file uploads and sharing changes, mail gateway records of outbound attachments, and endpoint events for removable media and archive creation. Detection in isolation is hard because organisations legitimately move large amounts of data to those same services every day, and because the most damaging exfiltration is often small and targeted, such as a handful of documents leaving through an approved channel. Analysis therefore depends on joining collection and exfiltration evidence, comparing transfer volume against the account's own history and peer group, and knowing which destinations and volumes are normal for each business function before an incident begins.
objectives: Describe the main exfiltration channels and the specific telemetry each generates at the network, cloud, mail, and endpoint boundary.
Analyse transfer volume, direction, timing, and destination reputation against per-user and per-host baselines.
Join collection evidence to exfiltration evidence to establish a defensible data-loss narrative.
Explain how egress control, data loss prevention, and cloud sharing restrictions complement each other and where each fails.
Recognise low-volume targeted exfiltration that will not trigger volumetric thresholds and design detections for it.
Draft the containment decision points that determine whether an in-progress transfer can actually be stopped.
